messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
I want to stage an Estes D12-5 to an Estes C6-5. It should get to roughly 310 m. Every section needs to land under 15 ft/s. Our field sits about 1,300 m above sea level.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: two stages, motors fixed. Booster is an Estes D12-5, sustainer an Estes C6-5. Apogee roughly 310 m, within about 5%. Every section lands under 15 ft/s: 15 * 0.3048 = 4.57 m/s. The field is about 1,300 m above sea level, so I pass site altitude 1300 m. Wind and rail are not stated, so 2 m/s and a 1.5 m rail, launched vertical. Both stages need their own recovery.
2. Feasibility: 310 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 310) = 78 m/s. A D12 plus a C6 is more than enough impulse, and thin air at 1300 m makes it easier, so the airframe should not be a minimum-diameter dart. The D12-5 coast is the staging delay: the stack stays together until that ejection, then the C6 lights. Confirming both motors.

2. Feasibility: the D12 is 16.8 N*s, 10.4 N, burn 1.61 s, 24 mm, and 5 s is a listed delay. The C6 is 8.8 N*s, 4.8 N, burn 1.83 s, 18 mm, also with a 5 s delay. Together that is 16.8 + 8.8 = 25.6 N*s. Liftoff thrust is only the D12. On a guessed 0.18 kg stack, thrust-to-weight = 10.4 / (0.18 * 9.81) = 5.89, above 3. The C6 does not light until 5 s after D12 burnout, which is the D12-5 ejection.
3. Size: rail acceleration (10.4 - 1.77) / 0.18 = 47.9 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 47.9 * 1.5) = 12.0 m/s on average thrust. The D12 spikes to 29.7 N, so the real exit should clear 15 m/s. Sustainer descent mass is about 0.08 kg. At 4 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.08 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4^2) = 0.100 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.100 / 3.1416) = 0.357 m. A 0.40 m sustainer chute and a 0.36 m booster chute should both stay under 4.57 m/s. The C6-5 then opens the upper chute about 1.83 + 5 = 6.8 s after staging.
4. Draft: both stages are 42 mm cardboard. Sustainer on top with the C6-5, ignition delay 5 s, and its own fins and chute. Booster below with the D12-5, separation on ejection, its own fins and chute. Site altitude 1300 m, wind left at 2 m/s.

4. Check: the simulator gives 591.7 m. Against 310 m that is (591.7 - 310) / 310 = 0.909, about 91% high. Margin is 0.21 cal at rail exit and through the burn, under 1.0, so the stack is not stable. Both sections land softly: sustainer 3.1 m/s and booster 3.2 m/s, under 4.57. Rail exit 21.7 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.0. Staging did what the delays say: booster chute at 6.7 s, sustainer chute at 13.5 s right on apogee. Liftoff mass is only 0.132 kg, lighter than my 0.18 kg guess, and the site is at 1300 m. Both of those push the apogee up.
5. Fix: 591.7 m and 0.21 cal have the same cause, a light stack with the motors in the tail. Adding 0.10 kg of nose weight in the sustainer. That is 0.10 / 0.132 = 0.758 of the current liftoff mass, up front, so the CG moves forward and the coast gets shorter. Motors, delays and chutes stay. Landing was 3.1 m/s, so there is room under 4.57 m/s for the extra mass.

4. Check: the simulator gives 179.1 m. That is under 310 m: (310 - 179.1) / 310 = 0.422, about 42% low. The 0.10 kg weight overshot. Margin is now 2.73 cal at rail exit and 1.58 cal in the burn, so stability is fixed. The booster lands at 3.2 m/s. The sustainer is not a real recovery: flight time equals the 13.5 s ejection, landing speed is 0.0 m/s, and the tool warns that the ejection and the chute happened after landing. The upper stage was on the ground before the C6-5 fired. Rail exit 17.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 4.6.
5. Fix: 179.1 m is the miss, and the late chute is the same problem, a flight that died before 13.5 s. Cutting the nose weight from 0.10 kg to 0.06 kg. The bare stack flew 591.7 m and this one flew 179.1 m, so 310 m sits between them, closer to the heavier end. Margin was 2.73 cal, so losing 0.04 kg of nose mass should leave it above 1 cal. Delays and chutes stay.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulator gives 276.2 m. Against 310 m that is (310 - 276.2) / 310 = 0.109, about 11% low, outside the 5% band. The sustainer lands at 4.6 m/s, just over the 4.57 m/s limit. The booster lands at 3.2 m/s and passes. Margin is 2.05 cal at the rail and 1.42 cal in the burn. The upper chute opens at 13.5 s, 13.5 - 10.24 = 3.3 s after apogee, and the tool warns of a 43.4 m/s opening. It did open before the ground this time. Rail exit 18.9 m/s, thrust-to-weight 5.5.
5. Fix: 276.2 m is the altitude miss, and the 4.6 m/s landing is the heavy sustainer under a chute sized for less mass. Cutting the nose weight from 0.06 kg to 0.045 kg. Between 0.10 kg and 0.06 kg the apogee rose from 179.1 m to 276.2 m, so a smaller step back up the same slope should land near 310 m and lighten the sustainer enough to get under 4.57 m/s. Margin is 2.05 cal, so 0.015 kg less nose mass will not drop it through 1 cal.

4. Check: the simulator gives 359.0 m. Against 310 m that is (359.0 - 310) / 310 = 0.158, about 16% high, outside the 5% band. The weight cut went too far. Everything else passes. Sustainer landing 4.2 m/s and booster landing 3.2 m/s are under 4.57. Margin is 1.71 cal at the rail and 1.33 cal in the burn. Rail exit 19.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 6.0. The upper chute still opens at 13.5 s, after apogee at 11.67 s, with a 34.5 m/s opening warning. That warning is not a failed gate, and the delay is fixed by the C6-5.
5. Fix: 359.0 m is the miss. At 0.060 kg the apogee was 276.2 m and at 0.045 kg it is 359.0 m, so 310 m is between them. Setting the nose weight to 0.054 kg, which is 0.045 + (0.060 - 0.045) * (359.0 - 310) / (359.0 - 276.2) = 0.054 kg. Chutes, motors and fins stay.

4. Check: the simulator gives 308.8 m. Against 310 m that is (310 - 308.8) / 310 = 0.0039, under half a percent, inside the 5% band. Sustainer landing is 4.4 m/s and booster landing is 3.2 m/s, both under 4.57. Margin is 1.93 cal at the rail and 1.4 cal through the burn. Rail exit 19.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 5.7. The D12-5 separates the booster at 6.7 s and the C6-5 opens the sustainer chute at 13.5 s. Apogee is at 10.9 s, so the upper opening is late and the tool warns of 39.6 m/s. The chute still opens in the air, and the touchdown speed is the 4.4 m/s under the canopy. Site altitude in the output is 1300 m.
5. Fix: no further change; altitude, both landings and the margin all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 308.8 m is close to 310 m only because the nose weight is 0.054 kg. A few grams either way moved this stack between 276 m and 359 m, so the real build has to be weighed. The sustainer landing at 4.4 m/s is 0.17 m/s under the 4.57 m/s cap. The 39.6 m/s opening is rough on a thin plastic chute; the C6-5 delay is what the request fixed, so the opening cannot be earlier without changing the motor. Thin air at 1300 m is already in the run. Drift was 180 m for the sustainer and 125 m for the booster.

Two-stage cardboard rocket: Estes D12-5 booster to an Estes C6-5 sustainer, with 0.054 kg of nose weight.
At a 1,300 m site the simulator gives 309 m. Both sections land under 4.57 m/s (4.4 and 3.2), with 1.93 cal of margin.
